reynolds-figure.intro: Reynolds, 1883. Press Start, then open the valve one step at a time and watch the dye.
reynolds-figure.big: Smooth or chaotic is decided by one number, Re = ρVD/μ: the water’s inertia against its viscosity.

steps.title: Still tank
steps.hint: Valve nearly shut, and the tank has settled for hours. The dye leaves the needle as one straight thread.

steps.title: Open slowly
steps.hint: Re climbs past 2,000. In a still tank small disturbances die out, so the thread mostly holds.

steps.title: Past the onset
steps.hint: Push Re past what this tank can hold. The thread wavers, bursts into eddies and fills the tube, and the friction dot jumps from 64/Re up to Blasius.

steps.title: Stir the tank
steps.hint: Back to about Re 3,000 with a clean tube, then stir. Disturbed water trips the tube near 2,000 to 3,000 instead of holding on.

steps.title: Warm the water
steps.hint: Viscosity halves between 20 and 50 °C, so the same valve opening gives about twice the Re.

senarmont-plate.intro: Sénarmont, 1847: a hot needle on a waxed crystal plate. Press Start and watch the shape of the melt.
senarmont-plate.big: In a crystal, heat can prefer a direction: thermal conductivity is a tensor, not a single number.

steps.title: Glass
steps.hint: Fused silica is glass, with no crystal lattice. Heat spreads equally in every direction, so the wax melts in a circle.

steps.title: Quartz, across c
steps.hint: A Z-cut quartz plate looks straight down the c axis. Both directions in the plate are a axes, so the melt is still a circle.

steps.title: Quartz, along c
steps.hint: A Y-cut plate contains the c axis. Quartz conducts 10.4 W/m·K along c and 6.2 across it, so the melt stretches into an ellipse.

steps.title: Turn the crystal
steps.hint: Turn the stage: the ellipse turns with the plate, not with you. The preferred direction belongs to the crystal.

steps.title: Read the ratio
steps.hint: The axes settle near a/b = √(10.4 ÷ 6.2) ≈ 1.30: the shape is set by the two conductivities alone.

tem-anatomy.intro: A 200 kV electron microscope, cut in half. Press Start and follow the electrons down the column.
tem-anatomy.big: One column, two pictures: the lenses decide whether the screen shows the specimen or its diffraction pattern.

steps.title: The beam
steps.hint: Electrons leave a tungsten filament at 200 kV, moving at 0.695 c with a wavelength of 2.5 pm. Two condenser lenses shape them into a parallel beam.

steps.title: Bright field
steps.hint: The objective aperture passes only the direct beam. Grains that diffract strongly send their electrons elsewhere and look dark.

steps.title: Dark field
steps.hint: Centre the aperture on a diffracted beam instead: now only the grains that diffract light up.

steps.title: Diffraction
steps.hint: Change the intermediate lens and the screen shows the back focal plane: aluminium’s spot pattern, one pair of spots per set of planes.

steps.title: Nanoparticles
steps.hint: Gold nanoparticles lie at every angle, so the spots smear into rings.

steps.title: Amorphous
steps.hint: Amorphous carbon has no long-range order: only diffuse halos are left.

steps.title: Take it apart
steps.hint: Explode the column to see every lens, aperture and coil that shaped the beam.

transport-lab-upgrade.intro: The course's Transport Laboratory solver and an upgraded one, on the same grid, both checked against the exact answer. Press Start.
transport-lab-upgrade.big: Same grid, same physics: how a scheme writes its face fluxes and its time step decides whether the answer is smeared, exact, or blows up.

steps.title: Pure conduction
steps.hint: With no flow the lab's explicit scheme is already accurate: both sit on the exact solution, a few hundredths of a kelvin off, and the lab's can even edge ahead.

steps.title: Add a flow
steps.hint: Turn on a 10 % flow. First-order upwind adds numerical diffusion of about uΔx/2, so the orange rings smear away from the line while the violet dots stay on it.

steps.title: Past the limit
steps.hint: At 30 % flow the explicit step breaks its own stability limit: C + 2r ≈ 1.09, above 1, and the field blows up within a second. The upgraded scheme stays within 2 K and settles to a few hundredths.

steps.title: Exact at steady state
steps.hint: The exponential scheme uses the exact 1D profile between cells, so the steady answer is exact at any Péclet number: its error sits at round-off, around 10⁻¹² K.

steps.title: Bigger steps
steps.hint: Crank–Nicolson is stable at any step. Back at 10 % flow, the upgrade now takes steps 16 times longer and is still the more accurate of the two.
